steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our HCI paper on how voice assistants fail multicultural users, the harms those failures cause, and communication repair designs that reduce harm. Cover the motivation, our research questions, contributions, and our methodological stance.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Voice assistants are growing but underserve many user groups
2. Our aim and research questions
3. Novelty and contributions
4. Methodological stance: centering excluded users
5. Closing: from documentation to generative design

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Motivation
- over 48% of U.S. adults expected to use voice assistants within two years; nearly half
- still fail several user groups
- documented underserved groups: women; multilingual and multicultural individuals; people of color
- inequitable speech recognition error rates -> utility, functionality, emotional wellbeing
- users code-switch (alter accent/language variety) to be understood
- disrespect: names of important cultural figures not understood
- users not prioritized in design -> frustrated, anxious, and/or angry

2. Aim / RQs
- move past documentation toward addressing inequities
- users' conceptualizations of assistants (Amazon Alexa, Apple Siri, Google Assistant, Bixby) -> RQ1
- taxonomy of harms -> RQ2; harms may extend to any misrecognized user
- social psychology + insights -> communication repair strategies -> RQ3

3. Contributions
- first paper: (1) sociotechnical taxonomy of harms for socially inequitable aspect of voice assistants (2) communication repair strategies for multicultural users
- HCI research agenda: harm reduction and repair
- 16 interviews / design workshops
- insights on conceptualizing/anthropomorphizing; 6 distinct harms; preliminary harm-reducing repair designs and guidelines

4. Methods stance
- privilege voices of historically excluded users
- focus on quality-of-service harms + downstream harms
- alternative illustrative methodologies: more just power distribution; [quote: help readers adopt someone else's gaze]

5. Closing
- all users experience errors, not the same subjective experience
- beyond documenting/taxonomizing -> generative practice for error recovery
- designs may benefit all voice assistant users

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Over 48% of adults in the United States are expected to use voice assistants within the next two years, which is nearly half of the adult U.S. population. But even though they are growing fast with consumers, voice assistants still don't meet the needs of several user groups. Scholars have more and more documented the ways that voice assistants underserve diverse populations, including but not limited to women, multilingual and multicultural individuals, and people of color. This work has shown how inequitable rates of speech recognition errors cause differences not just in utility and functionality, but also in emotional wellbeing. Users have said that they have to code-switch (i.e. change their speech to a different accent or language variety when they talk to their assistant) just so it understands their commands. They have also reported cases of disrespect, where their assistant doesn't understand the names of important cultural figures. In the end, if you are a user who is not prioritized in the design process, you will likely feel frustrated, anxious, and/or angry about your experiences.

In our work, we want to move past just documenting inequities, and start to think about how they can be readily addressed. To do this, first we capture how users conceptualize their voice assistants, including users of Amazon Alexa, Apple Siri, Google Assistant, and Bixby. (RQ1: How do multicultural voice assistant users’ frustrations impact their conceptualizations of their voice assistant?) Then we create a taxonomy of harms that users have experienced with their voice assistant. (RQ2: What specific harms arise from multicultural users’ error-prone interactions with their voice assistant?) Even though this inquiry is specific, the harms we documented could extend to any user who has been misrecognized by their voice assistant. We combine all these insights with a strong body of work from social psychology to create communication repair strategies that address potential user harms. (RQ3: What conversational UX designs may minimize the harm inflicted by error-prone voice assistants?)

- Novelty: first paper applying sociotechnical taxonomy of harms to inequitable aspect of voice assistants; repair strategies for multicultural users; HCI harm reduction/repair agenda
  - 16 interviews / design workshops
  - contributions: conceptualization/anthropomorphization insights; 6 distinct harms; preliminary harm-reducing repair designs and guidelines
- Methods stance: privilege excluded users; quality-of-service harms + downstream harms; illustrative methodologies (power distribution; "adopt someone else’s gaze")
- Closing: errors universal but experienced differently; generative practice; designs benefit all users

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Over 48% of adults in the United States are expected to use voice assistants within the next two years, which is nearly half of the adult U.S. population. But even though they are growing fast with consumers, voice assistants still don't meet the needs of several user groups. Scholars have more and more documented the ways that voice assistants underserve diverse populations, including but not limited to women, multilingual and multicultural individuals, and people of color. This work has shown how inequitable rates of speech recognition errors cause differences not just in utility and functionality, but also in emotional wellbeing. Users have said that they have to code-switch (i.e. change their speech to a different accent or language variety when they talk to their assistant) just so it understands their commands. They have also reported cases of disrespect, where their assistant doesn't understand the names of important cultural figures. In the end, if you are a user who is not prioritized in the design process, you will likely feel frustrated, anxious, and/or angry about your experiences.

In our work, we want to move past just documenting inequities, and start to think about how they can be readily addressed. To do this, first we capture how users conceptualize their voice assistants, including users of Amazon Alexa, Apple Siri, Google Assistant, and Bixby. (RQ1: How do multicultural voice assistant users’ frustrations impact their conceptualizations of their voice assistant?) Then we create a taxonomy of harms that users have experienced with their voice assistant. (RQ2: What specific harms arise from multicultural users’ error-prone interactions with their voice assistant?) Even though this inquiry is specific, the harms we documented could extend to any user who has been misrecognized by their voice assistant. We combine all these insights with a strong body of work from social psychology to create communication repair strategies that address potential user harms. (RQ3: What conversational UX designs may minimize the harm inflicted by error-prone voice assistants?)

As far as we know, this is the first paper that (1) applies a sociotechnical taxonomy of harms specifically to the socially inequitable aspect of voice assistants and (2) provides communication repair strategies made with the unique needs of multicultural users in mind. These strategies are part of an important HCI research agenda toward harm reduction and repair. Through a study with 16 interviews / design workshops with multicultural voice assistant users, our paper makes these novel research contributions:

- We give new insights about how multilingual and multicultural users who are underserved by voice assistants conceptualize and anthropomorphize voice assistants.
- We outline 6 distinct harms that inequitable voice assistant interactions can cause.
- We offer preliminary designs and guidelines for harm-reducing conversational repair that fit both users’ preferences and prior research in social psychology.

Our work tries to privilege the voices of users who have historically been left out of the product development lifecycle. We did this by focusing on purpose on harms that these users experience disproportionately (i.e. quality-of-service harms) and by digging deeper to find the downstream harms of these top-level harm categories. We also chose alternative illustrative methodologies to encourage a more just power distribution between the research facilitator and each participant, and to help the research community that receives this paper “adopt someone else’s gaze”.

All users experience errors, but not everyone has the same subjective error experience. We go beyond just documenting perceptions and taxonomizing harms, and move toward a generative practice that helps improve the error recovery experience. The design directions we suggest are grounded in an investigation with multicultural users, but they may be deployed for the benefit of all voice assistant users.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Over 48% of adults in the United States are expected to use voice assistants within the next two years — nearly half of the adult U.S. population [1]. Despite their rapid consumer growth, however, voice assistants still fail to meet the needs of several user groups. Scholars have increasingly documented the ways in which voice assistants underserve diverse populations, including but not limited to women [2], multilingual and multicultural individuals [3], and people of color [4,5]. This body of work has revealed how inequitable rates of speech recognition errors lead to differences not only in utility and functionality, but also in emotional wellbeing [4]. Users have reported having to code-switch (i.e. alter their speech to a different accent or language variety when speaking with their assistant) simply to have it understand their commands [6]. They have also reported instances of disrespect, in which their assistant does not understand the names of important cultural figures [7]. Ultimately, if you are a user who is not prioritized in the design process, you are likely to feel frustrated, anxious, and/or angry about your experiences [8].

In our work, we aim to move past pure documentation of inequities and begin to consider how they may be readily addressed. To do this, we first capture users’ conceptualizations of their voice assistants, including users of Amazon Alexa, Apple Siri, Google Assistant, and Bixby. (RQ1: How do multicultural voice assistant users’ frustrations impact their conceptualizations of their voice assistant?) We then create a taxonomy of harms that users have experienced with their voice assistant. (RQ2: What specific harms arise from multicultural users’ error-prone interactions with their voice assistant?) Despite the specificity of this inquiry, the harms we documented have the potential to extend to any user who is misrecognized by their voice assistant. Combining these insights with a strong body of work from social psychology, we create communication repair strategies that address potential user harms. (RQ3: What conversational UX designs may minimize the harm inflicted by error-prone voice assistants?)

To our knowledge, this is the first paper that (1) applies a sociotechnical taxonomy of harms specifically to the socially inequitable aspect of voice assistants and (2) provides communication repair strategies with the unique needs of multicultural users in mind. These strategies subscribe to an important HCI research agenda toward harm reduction and repair. Through a study with 16 interviews / design workshops with multicultural voice assistant users, our paper makes the following novel research contributions:

- We provide new insights about how multilingual and multicultural users who are underserved by voice assistants conceptualize and anthropomorphize voice assistants.
- We outline 6 distinct harms that inequitable voice assistant interactions can inflict.
- We offer preliminary designs and guidelines for harm-reducing conversational repair that align with both users’ preferences and prior research in social psychology.

Our work aims to privilege the voices of users who have historically been excluded from the product development lifecycle. We did this by intentionally focusing on harms disproportionately experienced by these users (i.e. quality-of-service harms) and by digging deeper to identify the downstream harms of these top-level harm categories. We also selected alternative illustrative methodologies to encourage a more just power distribution between the research facilitator and each participant [9], and to help the research community receiving this paper “adopt someone else’s gaze” [10].

All users experience errors, but not everyone shares the same subjective error experience. We go beyond simply documenting perceptions and taxonomizing harms, and move toward a generative practice to help improve the error recovery experience. While grounded in an investigation with multicultural users, the design directions we suggest may be deployed for the benefit of all voice assistant users.
